cards.a: The TCP/IP model (the DoD/Internet model) describes the protocol stack actually developed for the Internet. It has four layers that map onto OSI's seven, and it is what Cisco/IOS speaks natively.

cards.q: List the four TCP/IP layers and the OSI layers each covers.
cards.a: Application covers OSI 7+6+5; Transport covers OSI 4; Internet (Network) covers OSI 3; Network Access (Link) covers OSI 2+1.

cards.q: What protocols are found at the TCP/IP Internet layer?
cards.a: IP (addressing and best-effort delivery), ICMP (errors/diagnosis), and IGMP (multicast group membership).

cards.q: What does the TCP/IP Network Access layer do?
cards.a: It puts IP packets into Ethernet frames, resolves IP to MAC via ARP, and actually transmits the bits. It covers OSI layers 2 and 1.

cards.q: What is the role of the TCP/IP Transport layer?
cards.a: It provides either TCP (reliable, connection-oriented, with flow and congestion control) or UDP (best-effort, connectionless), and it adds source and destination ports.
OSI 7,6,5 → TCP/IP Application; OSI 4 → Transport; OSI 3 → Internet; OSI 1,2 → Network Access.

cards.q: Why did TCP/IP win over pure OSI?
cards.a: OSI was reference-only, while TCP/IP shipped working software, and IP became the internetworking protocol everything was built upon.

cards.q: How many layers does the TCP/IP model have, per Cisco?
cards.a: Cisco traditionally teaches 4 layers. Some texts split it into 5 by separating the link and physical layers, so answer per the model specified in the question.

cards.q: Where does ARP live in the TCP/IP model?
cards.a: ARP lives at the Network Access (Link) layer, where it maps IP addresses to MAC addresses. Some exams place it at L3 or 'between layers', so know both contextual statements.

cards.q: Which layer does ICMP belong to?
cards.a: ICMP belongs to the Internet (Network) layer (L3) of the TCP/IP model, not to any other layer.

cards.q: Which protocols in the TCP/IP stack are unreliable and which adds reliability?
cards.a: IP, ICMP, and UDP are all unreliable (best-effort). Reliability is added by TCP or by applications.

cards.q: How do you verify network-layer reachability in practice?
cards.a: If ping works the L3 (Internet) layer is up; to test an L4 port you telnet to the host and port. This is the practical troubleshooting Cisco operators actually use.

cards.q: Give examples of Application-layer protocols in the TCP/IP model.
cards.a: HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS, DHCP, Telnet, SSH, and SNMP all sit at the TCP/IP Application layer.
